title: When Generosity Becomes Worship
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Discover how Millie anchored herself in God’s Word during difficult circumstances — and how that shapes her view of generosity.   The post  When Generosity Becomes Worship  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
summary_zh: 了解Millie在困难情况下如何在神的话语中扎根，以及这如何塑造她对慷慨的看法。《When Generosity Becomes Worship》一文首次出现在《Wycliffe》上。
title_zh: 当慷慨成为崇拜
content: What circumstances or experiences have shaped your life? For 93-year-old Millie (name changed), her testimony was shaped by the Great Depression and deep loss, but also by an enduring faith and a lifetime of seeing God’s faithfulness unfold. Every chapter of her story points back to the same truth: God’s Word sustained her. Millie was only six weeks old when her father suffered severe burns to his legs from an explosion. Overnight, Millie’s mother found herself caring for a newborn and a toddler while tending to a husband who was facing a long and painful recovery. Life was uncertain, and every dollar mattered. Yet when Millie looks back on those difficult years, she doesn’t first remember hardship. She remembers the faith that was demonstrated. Every Sunday morning, Millie’s mother would reach into a small jar where she saved a few quarters and hand one to Millie and one to her sister before they left for church. The family didn’t have much, but her parents believed that honoring God was never dependent on how much they had. “We were taught to tithe,” Millie recalled. “To give to the Lord because of His goodness to us.” Long before Millie understood phrases like “stewardship” or “planned giving,” she was learning a lesson that would shape the rest of her life: Generosity isn’t born out of abundance; it grows from trusting the one who provides. See how God is using the generosity of one group of friends to impact Bible translation → The Scripture Millie Carried Through the Years As Millie grew older, that foundation of faith continued to guide her. She married a godly man, and they centered their efforts around family, teaching and serving others. Both were educators, and they poured themselves into the lives of children while also remaining deeply involved in their church and community. Together, the couple experienced the joys of raising a family. But they also walked through a devastating loss. While Millie was pregnant with their younger son, the couple’s 7-year-old daughter tragically died. It’s difficult to imagine the depth of grief that Millie endured. Through her pain, she turned to God and His Word for comfort. Even now, decades later, she is still anchored by the promises found in Scripture. One particular passage resonates with Millie deeply: You will keep in perfect peace all who trust in you, all whose thoughts are fixed on you! Trust in the LORD always, for the LORD GOD is the eternal Rock. — Isaiah 26:3-4 (NLT) For Millie, Scripture was what met her in her grief, strengthened her through suffering and continued to anchor and guide her throughout the next chapters of her life. This past Easter, Mille’s family experienced another tragic event — her son was involved in a head-on collision. Thankfully he survived but was hospitalized and treated for serious injuries. Millie believes the Lord’s presence was unmistakable in the moments that followed this event. A Gift Rooted in Gratitude Not long after her son’s accident, Millie received a mailing from Wycliffe Foundation that included information about charitable gift annuities. For Millie, this felt like an invitation and an opportunity to respond to God’s faithfulness through generosity. A charitable gift annuity was not a completely new concept to Millie. Through family members connected with Faith Comes By Hearing (a Wycliffe partner organization), she learned about this unique giving option and appreciated that it could provide her with a lifetime income while also supporting a ministry she cared deeply about. When she received the information about charitable gift annuities, she saw it as another opportunity to worship the Lord and express her gratitude for His protection and provision. Millie reached out to Wycliffe Foundation, and Michael Occhipinti, senior gift planning advisor, quickly connected with her. 是什么环境或经历决定了你的生活? 对于93岁的米莉(名字变了)来说,她的证词是被大萧条和严重损失所塑造的,但也是一种持久的信仰和一生目睹上帝的忠诚发展。 她的故事的每一章都指向同样的真理:上帝的话支撑了她.

米莉只有六个星期大,当她的父亲在爆炸中腿部严重烧伤。 一夜之间,米莉的母亲发现自己在照顾一个新生儿和幼儿,同时照顾一个面临长期痛苦康复的丈夫。 生活是不确定的,每一美元都很重要。 但当米莉回顾那些艰难的岁月时,

她记得所表现的信仰. 每周日早上,米莉的母亲会到达一个小罐子,在那里她保存了几分钱,在他们出发去教堂之前,将一张交给米莉,一张交给她的妹妹. 她的父母认为尊重上帝永远不取决于他们拥有多少。 米莉回忆说,“我们被教导了十分之一。”

以至报应我们的主。 早在米莉明白“偷窥”或“计划施舍”等短语之前,她就已经吸取了将塑造其余生的教训:慷慨并非由丰产而生;它从信任提供者而增长。

看上帝如何利用一群朋友的慷慨影响圣经的翻译 – 《圣经·米莉》在米莉变老的岁月里载着她,这种信仰的基础继续引导着她. 她嫁给了一个虔诚的人,他们围绕家庭,教学和为他人服务而集中了自己的努力.

两人都是教育工作者,他们投入到儿童生活中,同时也深入参与他们的教会和社区。 夫妇们一起经历了养育家庭的快乐. 但他们也经历了毁灭性的损失。 Milie怀了年幼的儿子,

很难想象米莉承受的悲痛有多深。 通过她的痛苦,她转而向上帝和上帝的话求慰. 即使现在,几十年之后,她仍然以圣经中的承诺为依托。 一个特别的段落与米莉深刻的共鸣:所有信任你的人,你都将在完美的和平中守住,他们的思想都固定在你身上!

相信耶和华,因为耶和华是永恒的磐石。 以赛亚26:3-4 (NLT)对米莉来说,圣经是她在悲痛中遇见她,通过苦难使她更加坚强,并继续支撑和引导她整个下半生。 过去复活节,米尔的家人经历了另一个悲惨事件——她的儿子卷入了一次正面碰撞.

幸好他幸存下来,但住院治疗严重受伤。 Milie认为,在事件发生之后的那一刻,上帝的出现是无可置疑的。 Millie在儿子出事不久后收到Wycliffe基金会的邮件,

对米莉来说,这感觉像是一次邀请和机会,通过慷慨回应上帝的忠诚. 慈善礼物年金对米莉来说并不是全新的概念.

她通过与Faith Comes Booth(一个Wycliffe伙伴组织)有关的家庭成员了解到这一独特的赠与选择,并意识到这一选择能为她提供终身收入,同时支持她深爱的部委。

当她收到有关慈善礼物年金的信息时,她认为这是又一次机会,可以崇拜主,并对他的保护和供养表示感谢. 米莉联系了威克利夫基金会,高级礼品规划顾问迈克尔·奥西平蒂(Michael Occhipinti)迅速与她联系. 在整个过程中,他在她祷告地考虑她的下一步时与她同行。

content: An IMB missionary among the Deaf records a Bible story in sign language. IMB Photo Every dollar you give to the Lottie Moon offering goes to support missionaries like Noah Lewis who live and serve among the lost. Will you consider giving today? Noah Lewis couldn’t help signing along with a worship song playing in the background as Deaf friends gathered in his home for dinner. The International Mission Board appoints missionaries who are both Deaf and hearing to serve among the global Deaf. Many missionaries learn sign language for the first time, while others use their American Sign Language to more quickly learn global sign languages. IMB Photo The International Mission Board missionary was sitting in the living room with his roommate and two friends while others prepared food nearby. As a young, single adult, simply opening the doors to his home in the Middle East has created some of his most fruitful opportunities for gospel conversations. That evening, Lewis was stirred to worship the Lord. “I just love worshiping in sign language because it’s a full-body experience,” Lewis said. Lewis, who is hearing, began signing the song in American Sign Language. Across the room, one of his Muslim friends watched intently. When the song ended, his friend told him it was beautiful and asked to see another. Lewis explained that Christians use songs to worship God. His friend compared what he had seen to hearing the Islamic call to prayer. The exchange opened an opportunity for Lewis to explain Christian worship and why Christians worship Jesus. When his friend asked to see more, Lewis continued signing songs from the playlist. “He was just really captivated by it,” Lewis said. “It really felt like in that moment the Spirit was working in his heart.” The conversation did not end with a profession of faith. Instead, it became another step in a friendship where Lewis has watched spiritual curiosity grow over time. During Ramadan, the same friend asked about fasting. On another night, he asked how Christians pray. Each question has allowed Lewis to explain what Christians believe and why he follows Jesus. Those conversations reflect much of Lewis’ ministry. He has served in the Middle East for nearly a year and a half, spending much of his time learning sign language and building relationships in the local Deaf community. Learning sign language, like learning any language, requires time, practice and immersion in the community that uses it. For Lewis, that process has looked different from the experience of missionaries who can spend several hours each day in a formal language school. There are no comparable sign language centers where he serves, so much of his language learning happens through relationships with Deaf friends. Although Lewis has not had a dedicated language tutor since arriving on the field, personal relationships help him develop a strong conversational understanding of the sign language used where he serves. The process has also drawn him more deeply into the Deaf community he came to reach. “I want to genuinely learn about their language,” he said. “I want to be friends with them. I want to know who they are.” As Lewis’ ability to communicate grows, relationships deepen and opportunities to share the gospel follow. Even when he doesn’t know the exact sign he needs, friends help him find ways to communicate biblical truths. Lewis has learned to faithfully use the language he has while continuing to grow in his ability to communicate the gospel clearly. An IMB worker among the Deaf records a Bible story. Generous giving to the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering supports missions among the global Deaf. IMB Photo When the plan disappeared That dependence on God came into clearer focus during a recent trip to Central Asia. Lewis currently lives and serves in the Middle East, but he arrived on the field with a long-term desire to serve in Central Asia. 一名IMB在聋人中的传教士用手语记录圣经故事. IMB照片 你给洛蒂月球的每一美元 都用来支持传教士 比如诺亚·刘易斯 你会考虑今天给钱吗? 当聋人朋友聚集在家中吃饭时,

国际代表团委员会任命聋人和听力传教士在全球聋人中任职。 许多传教士首次学习手语,而其他传教士则使用他们的美国手语更快地学习全球手语.

IMB照片 国际传教委员会传教士与他的室友和两个朋友坐在客厅里,而其他人则在附近准备食物. 作为一个年轻、单身的成年人,只要打开通往他在中东的家的大门,就为他的福音对话创造了一些最富有成果的机会。 当晚,刘易斯被激起崇拜主.

「我只是喜欢手语崇拜, 正在听话的刘易斯开始用美国手语签署歌曲. 在房间里,他的一个穆斯林朋友故意观看。 歌曲结束的时候,他的朋友告诉他这很美丽,并请求见另一首. 刘易斯解释说,基督徒使用歌曲来崇拜上帝.

他的朋友比较了他所看到的听到的伊斯兰祈祷的呼声. 这次交流为刘易斯解释基督教崇拜和基督徒为何崇拜耶稣提供了机会. 当他的朋友要求看到更多时,刘易斯继续从播放列表上签名歌曲. 刘易斯说:“他只是被它迷住了。”

“在那个时刻,精神确实在他心中发挥作用。” 对话没有以信仰职业结束。 相反,它成为友谊的又一个步骤,刘易斯目睹了精神好奇心随时间推移而增长. 斋月期间,同友问斋事. 在另一个晚上,他问基督徒如何祈祷.

每个问题都让刘易斯解释基督徒相信什么,为什么他跟随耶稣. 这些谈话反映了刘易斯部的许多情况。 他在中东服务了近一年半,花了很多时间学习手语,在当地聋人社区建立关系.

学习手语,就像学习任何语言一样,需要时间,练习和沉浸在使用手语的社区中. 对刘易斯来说,这一进程与传教士的经历不同,传教士可以每天在一所正式语言学校中度过几个小时。

他所服务的手语中心并不存在类似的手语中心,所以他的许多语言学习都是通过与聋人朋友的关系发生的. 虽然刘易斯自到达球场后便没有专门的语言辅导员,但个人关系帮助他发展出对他所服务的手语的强烈的对话理解.

这一过程还使他更深入地融入了他所接触的聋人社区。 他说:“我想真正了解他们的语言。” “我想与他们成为朋友。 我想知道他们是谁。” 随着刘易斯沟通能力的增长,关系加深,分享福音的机会随之而来。

即使他不知道自己需要什么具体标志, 刘易斯学会了忠实使用他拥有的语言,同时继续增强他明确传达福音的能力. 一个IMB工人在聋人中记录了一个圣经故事. 慷慨地给洛蒂月亮圣诞节 提供全球聋人中的支持任务

title_zh: 俄亥俄州派遣庆祝活动确认33名IMB传教士为全球服务
content: Participants at the IMB Sending Celebration on Nov. 9, 2026, celebrated God's faithfulness in sending 33 new missionaries to the nations. Held at the Sugarcreek campus of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, the event launched the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio annual gathering. For security reasons, some newly appointed missionaries are not publicly identified. IMB Photo God continues to call His people to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. During a Sending Celebration Nov. 9 at the Sugarcreek Campus of First Baptist Church Kettering, near Dayton, Ohio, 33 International Mission Board missionaries stood before family, friends and supporters, affirming their obedience to that call. Trustees of the IMB appointed the fully supported missionaries who represent 10 states – including two candidates from Ohio – and many Southern Baptist churches committed to sending and sustaining those called by God to go to the mission field. Senior Pastor Chad Keck welcomed those in attendance, sharing his appreciation for the partnership with Southern Baptist churches to cooperatively send and support missionaries. The Sending Celebration is meeting in conjunction with the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio. Chad Keck, senior pastor of First Baptist Kettering near Dayton, Ohio, left, and Jeremy Westbrook, executive director-treasurer of the State Convention of Baptists in Ohio, right, welcome guests gathered for the IMB Sending Celebration, which kicked off the convention’s annual gathering. IMB Photo Among those who shared their stories include a couple who answered an unexpected call later in life, a couple who are returning to Albania and to people they could not forget; and a couple who moved from welcoming the nations in Canada to going to Fiji. All of them shared their stories before the Sending Celebration. Unexpected invitation to go On Dec. 5, 2025, what seemed like an ordinary FaceTime call became a turning point for Rob Boss. As he spoke with his daughter, Hannah, during her IMB training, Rob sensed God speaking clearly to his heart: “You can do this too.” The impression was unexpected. After decades of writing, Christian education, seminary teaching and active support of missions, overseas service had never been part of Rob and Stephanie Boss’ plans. “It wasn’t an audible voice, but it was so clear,” Rob said. “It was Him. It was so kind and so gentle and so encouraging.” The moment drove him to his knees in surrender. When Stephanie came home later that day, he told her he believed God was calling them to the nations. Her response was immediate. “Thrilled is the right answer,” she said. The next day, the couple contacted the IMB and began the application process. Though missions had long been part of their family’s story, Rob and Stephanie Boss sensed God leading them to overseas service while encouraging their daughter, Hannah, during her missionary training. Sent by Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, Texas, they are now headed to Colombia, where they will serve through theological education. IMB Photo Looking back, the Bosses see the Lord’s hand preparing them long before they realized where He was leading. “God brought us together in the summer of 1990 at Glorieta, New Mexico, where we met and married,” Stephanie said during the Sending Celebration. What followed was years of ministry, teaching, parenting and navigating life’s unexpected turns, which taught them to hold plans loosely and trust God completely. “We did not have a clue about what life held in front of us,” Stephanie said. “We just knew we wanted to follow the Lord.” Their calling also continues a family legacy. Rob’s mother served with the IMB in Africa after retirement, helping inspire Hannah’s service in South Korea. Now, three generations of the same family have answered God’s call to the nations. Rob and Stephanie expressed deep gratitude for their sending church, Wedgwood Baptist Church in Fort Worth, whose strong commitment to missions
content_zh:
2026年11月9日的IMB送信庆典的参与者,庆祝上帝向各国派遣33名新传教士的忠诚. 该活动在俄亥俄州代顿附近的第一浸信会Kettling的Sugarcreek校园举行,在俄亥俄州发起了浸信会州议会年会。 出于安全考虑,一些新任命的传教士没有公开身份.

IMB图片神继续呼叫 他的族人将福音传到地底 11月9日,在俄亥俄州代顿附近的第一浸信会Kettling教堂的Sugarcreek校区,33名国际传教委员会传教士站在家人、朋友和支持者面前,申明他们服从这一呼吁。

IMB的受托人任命了代表10个州的全力支持的传教士 — — 包括俄亥俄州的两名候选人 — — 以及许多南方浸信会教会承诺将那些被上帝召唤去传教的传教士送去并维持下去.

高级牧师Chad Keck欢迎与会者,与他一样感谢与美南浸信会教会合作派遣和支持传教士。 送教庆典会与俄亥俄州的浸信会州会议同时举行.

俄亥俄州代顿附近第一浸信会Ketting的资深牧师查德·凯克(Chad Keck)左翼,俄亥俄州浸信会执行董事兼创始人杰里米·韦斯特布鲁克(Jeremy Westbrook)右翼欢迎前来参加IMB送信庆典的来宾,这驱散了大会的年度集会。

在分享自己故事的人中,有一对夫妇在生活后期意外地接了电话,一对夫妇正在返回阿尔巴尼亚,一对夫妇无法忘记;一对夫妇从欢迎加拿大各国搬到斐济。 他们都分享了他们的故事 在送信庆典之前。 意外邀请 Dec 上。

5, 2025, 看起来像一个普通的FaceTime电话成为Rob Boss的转折点. 当他和他的女儿汉娜在IMB训练期间交谈时,罗布感应到上帝对他说的很清楚:“你也可以这样做。” 印象出乎意料。

经过几十年的写作、基督教教育、神学院教学和对使团的积极支持,海外服务从未成为罗布和斯蒂芬妮·博斯计划的一部分。 Rob说, “这不是一个声音, “这是他。 它是如此善良和温柔,如此鼓舞人心。” 那一刻,他被迫跪在地上投降。

当斯蒂芬妮当天晚些时候回家时,他告诉她,他相信上帝在召唤他们到各国. 她立即作出反应。 她说,“令人惊叹的是正确的答案。” 次日,夫妇联系IMB,开始了申请程序.

虽然传教团早就是他们家庭故事的一部分,但罗布和史蒂芬妮·博斯感知到,在传教团训练期间,他们带领他们到海外服务,同时鼓励他们的女儿汉娜。 由德克萨斯州沃思堡的韦奇伍德浸信会(Wedgwood Baptist Church)派遣,他们现在前往哥伦比亚,通过神学教育服务.

IMB照片回想起来,老板们看到主的手 在他们意识到在哪里之前很早就准备了 他是领导。 " 1990年夏天,上帝把我们带到了新墨西哥州格洛里埃塔,我们在那里相遇并结婚。 " Stephanie在送货庆典上说。

接下来是多年的教职、教职、养育和过着意想不到的转折,教他们松动计划,完全相信上帝。 Stephanie说:“我们不知道我们面前的生活是什么。” 我们只知道我们想跟随主。 他们的召唤也延续了家庭遗产。

罗布的母亲退休后在非洲为IMB效力,帮助激励汉娜在韩国服役. 现在,同一家庭的三代人响应了上帝向各国发出的呼吁。 Rob和Stephanie深表感谢他们派来的教会Worth堡的Wedgwood浸信会教堂,他们坚定致力于使命

title: IMB missionaries in place, prepared to encourage Senegal’s churches toward Youth Olympics outreach
summary: As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. content: A Senegalese Christian shares the gospel with event volunteers during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo As athletes and spectators from around the world fill the streets of Senegal for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, missionaries and local believers are praying the event will leave behind more than medals and memories. For Carson West, an International Mission Board missionary serving in Senegal, the Games represent a unique opportunity not only to engage visitors with the gospel but also to mobilize local churches to take a more active role in evangelism long after the Olympic flame is extinguished. “This is the first Olympic event ever held on the continent of Africa,” West said. “For us, it was an opportunity to ask, ‘What are we going to do with this?’” The Youth Olympic Games, which began Oct. 31 and end Nov. 13, are taking place across three host cities: Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. Event organizers expect nearly 2,700 athletes, ages 14-17, to participate in 35 sports and represent more than 200 delegations. The Games have drawn a million spectators, and West reported more than 6,000 event volunteers are staffing all the venues. With so many people gathering in Senegal, West and his team concentrated on preparing Senegalese churches for evangelistic opportunities. “We could run and hide, or we could do this thing,” West said, recalling an early conversation with teammates. “We decided we were going to do this thing.” The 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, is the first Olympic event held on the continent of Africa. IMB Photo West serves as team leader for IMB work in Senegal, where ministry efforts focus on three areas: gospel engagement, church advancement and community development. The Youth Olympic outreach naturally aligns with the first two priorities. “Our approach has been to mobilize the local church,” he said. “This is their backyard.” Instead of relying on a large influx of international volunteers, though there is one volunteer team from the United States serving, the strategy has centered on equipping local believers. Senegal has four Baptist churches in the greater Dakar area. Many leaders representing the congregations, as well as other ministry partners, participated in evangelism training designed specifically for the Games. Church leaders and ministry partners in Senegal participate in an evangelism training session specifically designed to share the gospel during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. IMB Photo A key outreach method involves trading commemorative pins, a familiar Olympic tradition. Volunteers use the exchange as a natural conversation starter before offering gospel-centered materials. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code connected to a digital engagement platform adapted from previous Olympic and World Cup outreaches. Visitors who scan the code are directed to online resources and can connect with trained digital responders. Experienced volunteers in the U.S. are helping provide follow-up conversations. “We’re building on strategies that have been used effectively in previous Olympic Games,” West said. “It’s an easy, non-intimidating way to start gospel conversations.” Trading commemorative pins is an Olympic tradition. Volunteers use these pins to start gospel-driven conversations during the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar. Each pin is accompanied by a card featuring a QR code that connects people to trained digital responders. IMB Photo The effort extends beyond Dakar. IMB teams and church partners are positioned in each of the three host cities. An IMB team, which includes three global missionary partners, is helping coordinate outreach efforts in Diamniadio, and an IMB team along with a Baptist church is organizing efforts in Saly. West believes the greatest potential impact may be felt not among international visitors but among Senegalese believers themselves. Senegal is approximately 95% Muslim and 0.2% evangelical. summary: When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. title_zh: IMB寻求教师、医护人员、商业专业人士担任传教士
content: IMB missionary Dr. Heidi Haun, left, checks on patients at Baptist Medical Centre in Nalerigu, Ghana. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. IMB missionary Glen Garner uses his business skills and experience as the logistics director for missionaries serving globally. He lives in Lima, Peru, with his wife, Shannon

IMB正在寻找其他教育者,比如波尔,他们愿意在任务领域运用自己的技能. IMB Photo Scott Ray是IMB全球部署的高级主任,他指出,许多传教士职位由于不属于传教士服务的传统观念而无人填补. 他说,专业技能既能提供实用的部委支助,也能进入传统传教签证难以获得的国家。 金融专业人员、兽医、医务工作者、派遣救济人员和其他人都有机会。 保健仍然是需求最有战略意义的领域之一。 全球卫生战略的IMB主任汤姆·希克斯(Tom Hicks)说,许多医疗专业人员对任务工作的看法是错误的. 他表示:「我们确实有个问题, 人们会选择出局, 事实上,Hicks说,全球许多地区正在越来越多地寻找家庭医学医生、实习医生、儿科医生、儿科护士、产科医生、物理治疗师、职业治疗师、语言病理学家和哺乳期咨询师。 这种需求在撒哈拉以南非洲尤为重要,那里的青年人口对儿科护理的需求日益增加。 在限制传教活动的国家,保健专业人员也提供了独特的优势。 「有职业价值的使团, 另一个经常被忽略的部是成员护理,重点是IMB传教士的精神、情感、心理和关系健康。 克里斯·马丁是IMB全球会员关怀的总监. Martin说,“会员关心传教士与那些传统上被认为是教会植树人或福音传教士的传教士站在一起并支持他们。” 担任这些角色的许多人来自咨询背景,帮助传教士应对压力、冲突、悲痛和其他挑战,这些挑战可能影响部委的长期效力。 马丁将他们的角色比作出埃及19号的Aaron和Hur,在战斗中举起摩西的手臂,强化了在前线服役的人. IMB传教士格伦·加纳(英语:Glen Garner)利用其作为在全球服务的传教士的后勤主任的业务技能和经验. 他和妻子香农住在秘鲁利马

title_zh: IMB传教士通过新信徒和当地教会看到神在工作
content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo That spring, Tara was baptized.

IMB照片已经过了20分钟 太阳正在下山,他们到处找,但他们只在公园里看到男人. 索菲亚是一位国际传教委员会传教士,他加入了另一位IMB传教士和一位南亚基督徒玛丽安. 他们去公园分享福音,但是接近一个他们穆斯林占多数的城市里的人是不可能的. 他们不停地走着看。 即使他们一言不发地回家,索菲亚也知道玛丽安会想再试一次. 这个在对穆斯林的不信任中长大的妇女,现在找了个公园,找一个穆斯林妇女来讲述耶稣. 当索菲亚第一次邀请她一起来时,玛丽安从未想象过一个穆斯林能够来认识耶稣. 但是他们越是出去分享福音 越是上帝软化了她的心 “有一天,我发现她在公园里独自分享,没有我,”索菲亚笑着说。 这些天,她经常分享——与同班同学,有人力车司机,公园里的妇女,当她能找到她们的时候. 上帝改变了玛丽安的心 他也可以改变这个走过公园。 " 于是,我们停下来了。 " 索菲亚说: " 祈祷说:"上帝啊,求你只给我们一个女人来说话。 " 然后他们发现她——一个独自坐在长凳上的女孩。 她看起来像当地其他保守的穆斯林妇女, 他们随意接近,不想吓到她。 苏菲亚说, 他们向她问候,并询问她的假期计划. 她的名字叫Tara, “你可能认为我穿得像穆斯林一样,”她说,“但实际上,在我心中,我离开了伊斯兰教。 索菲亚说:“我有点震惊,”听到一个陌生人这么大胆的发言。 Tara告诉他们她是一所保守的伊斯兰学校的大学生,但她已经对宗教产生了幻灭和不满. Tara说:「我不再相信伊斯兰教了。 没有上帝的知晓,她没有任何人可以祈祷,这让她孤独. 她从朋友那里寻找佛教和印度教, 甚至和无神论者会面, “你们认识任何基督徒吗?” 索菲亚问。 你们告诉我吧! 他们读到耶稣的出生,Tara更渴望更多。 当她问起教堂时,索菲亚描述了他们大约40名信徒的聚会,其中许多来自穆斯林背景. Tara继续学习。 Sophia和Maryam每周在咖啡店、茶店、Sophia家相会, 找到她最亲近的朋友 他们通过"约翰福音"阅读. 11月一日在一家咖啡店里,他们到达了井上撒玛利亚女人的通道,索菲亚注意到塔拉正在哭泣. “塔拉,我看到你有眼泪,”索菲亚说。 " 让我们停下来吧。 让我们谈谈。 当天,塔拉祈祷接受基督. 不久后,她想参观教堂,虽然担心信徒会如何用头巾接见她. “他们会爱你,”索菲亚告诉她。 “别担心。 Tara去了,受到欢迎。 80人收拾了索菲亚的公寓, 在房间对面,索菲亚看见了塔拉,身穿红色的圣诞外衣,像围巾和微笑被伸到她脸上. " Tara长大后非常保守——她家甚至不允许音乐. 现在她正在跳舞,用音乐和歌曲与我们一起崇拜上帝。 在南亚,玛丽安和一位当地牧师为新信徒塔拉施洗. IMB的传教士与当地的信徒和教会一起工作,完成"大委员会". IMB 相片 当年春天,塔拉被洗礼.

title_zh: 神通过IMB在意大利的传教士保持忠诚
content: The eastern face of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City in Rome, Italy, is famous for its central balcony from which popes give their papal addresses. Most people in Rome have at least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” IMB Photo In the city where Jason and Lizzy Davis serve, some steps have a lot of meaning. And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritual experience, a picture of a religion that asks people to earn their way to Jesus. “That’s really the opposite of what the gospel is. The gospel is Jesus saying, ‘No, you can’t do it . . . no matter how good you think you are,’” they said. Most people in Rome have at the very least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism, as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” Jason explained, “It’s where the Pope lives in the Vatican. It’s very much part of the religion and culture. It’s all intertwined here.” An ‘unavoidable’ call Jason and Lizzy are investing their lives as International Mission Board missionaries in Rome, Italy, to share the truth of the gospel. The Davises partner with national believers through a new church plant, and they’re seeking to plant more churches within the city. Lizzy said for her, the call to missions was unavoidable. “I grew up as a third culture kid, or a missionary kid. My parents were on the mission field, as were my grandparents, all with the International Mission Board.” Then her family moved to Virginia for her dad to work for IMB’s home office staff. As a middle schooler and high schooler, every time Lizzy heard about the need for the gospel to go forth, she felt a burden, a “burning” in her heart. She didn’t know what God would do with that, but she had a feeling she would see one day. Now, years later, she and Jason spend their time trying to find as many opportunities as they can to invite people into their home so they can share the hope of Jesus with them. That can mean Bible study or simply sharing a meal. ‘Completely lost’ Jason has been surprised by just how often people are willing to talk about faith. “You can get into spiritual conversations very quickly with people, especially if you’re just open and honest with them.” Lizzy shared that one of the easiest ways to do this is to be willing to let your day be interrupted. “That’s something I’ve seen Jason do firsthand in our neighborhood. He walks down the street, and everybody knows him because he stops and takes the time to ask them questions about their families, gets to know people, gets to know the newspaper stand guy and the guy at the fruit stand and the grocery store ladies.” She emphasized that caring about people is “what Christ would do.” The Davises, whose previous mission service prevents their photos from being published, live in a neighborhood of about 130,000 people. Their church of 15 people is the only evangelical congregation there. Lizzy said the area is “truly a lost, completely lost, dark neighborhood” with people who have never heard the gospel. Thousands more come to their area on a religious quest. The Davis family’s neighborhood is home to the Basilica Papale di San Paolo (the Papal Basilica of Saint Paul), one of the city’s four major basilicas. “So we get a lot of people coming on spiritual journeys, visiting our neighborhood, seeking some sort of spiritual experience. And oftentimes it’s just trying to earn their salvation,” she added. Jason described this environment as “a genuine need for people to actually hear the gospel and know that their sins can be forgiven and they can have an assurance of that.” IMB missionaries Jason and Liz

title_zh: 全球传教士合作伙伴通过IMB团队扩展福音工作
content: Rebeca Couto, a global missionary partner from the Azores islands, practices writing characters with her tutor in Japan. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto poses with her violin. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said. She continued, “Music is such a universal way to connect with people, and it’s so intuitive to pair that with the gospel and with God’s message to people’s hearts.” While she knew the Lord would somehow open a door for her to use the violin for kingdom work, she was at peace with the possibility that, for a season, she may not be as active in music. title_zh: IMB传教士使用家庭、咖啡馆、应用程序为西班牙的福音对话敞开大门
content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. From a missionary perspective, she believes the lab addresses a common challenge. “It’s hard to know sometimes as churches how to be a good sending church and how to support missionaries,” she sa

IMB Photo Leading the lab是IMB高级教会接触策略师布莱恩·伍滕(Bryan Wooten),他在看到传教士与本地教会之间需要更牢固的关系后发展出这个概念. 伍腾说,“一个派遣教会实验室是我们努力培养许多派遣教会的IMB。 ”他赞扬北美传教委员会开展了类似的活动并取得了成功。 实验室帮助教会理解伍腾所谓的教会参与途径:祈祷,合作,合作和发送. 虽然许多教堂忠实地祈祷,奉献和去,但他说送去需要更有意图的东西. 他解释说,“最后包括负责一个IMB传教士,在整个任职期间提供持续的鼓励、问责和精神关怀。” 在为期两天的活动期间,与会者聚集在白板周围,评价其教会的任务做法,查明优缺点并制订改进计划。 」伍腾说: “我们需要邀请教会自己做一些工作。” 与会者不是简单地听取演讲,而是通过祷告、赠送、短期访问、传教士评估和长期照料等实际问题开展工作。 Wooten说,教会总是告诉他最大的好处是清晰. 他说,“他们感谢对派遣教会的咨监委的澄清,以及我们的作用和责任。” 对于IMB的传教士彼得和凯蒂·威克斯来说,这种清晰度特别有价值. 他们与教会领袖一起参加了实验室. 他们的真名被更改以保护自己在东南亚的工作. 彼得说,“在这几天里,我宁愿呆在这里。” 凯蒂对培训的互动性表示赞赏. 我非常欣赏他们要求不同教会提供信息的方式, 从传教士的角度来看,她认为实验室解决了共同的挑战. title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. Mikah Young is serving overseas with the IMB. The work of the IMB is sustained through faithful giving to the Cooperative Program and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering ® . title_zh: IMB传教士在服务之旅中分享首尔的愿景
content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. Nobody advertised it as anything more than a place to practice English, but the room kept filling, and so did the conversations. The team’s work with students didn’t stop there. title_zh: 你就不能帮我吗?
content: Several times now, I have been out in creation with unbelievers, speaking to them of eternal matters, and, passing by a dying branch at the base of a tree, I have picked it up and said, “This is your life apart from Christ.” Speaking about their souls, Jesus’s illustration is irresistible. The conversation goes something like this: Jesus gives us this illustration. He looks you in the eye and says that he is the tree (to augment the illustration slightly), and you are the branch. Look up and see the branches above us, beautiful leaves waving, healthy in their vibrant greens, bearing evidence of life. And then there is this branch. Dry. Leafless. Withered. Why? Because it is detached from the source of its life. Cut off from the one it was made to have communion with. And so, it lies here, detached from its purpose and severed from the only thing that can make it flourish. Jesus claims to be man’s source. He claims to be the Tree to whom you belong. In relationship with him, you have life. Apart from him, he teaches, you spend life withering. I usually pause to let the claim have its proper space. I ask what they think of such an assertion. I give them an opportunity to respond. I have often expected indifference or offense, but I have consistently been met with quiet consideration or outright acknowledgment that such an illustration made sense to them. Or at least they would like to hear more. So I go on to wonder aloud with them. What is it like to be a branch fallen from the tree that is, as Jesus says, withering ? Don’t you know? Need we ask? The restlessness, the fatal dryness, the looming death. The reaching out to anything and everything for life — except for the tree standing beside and over us. Him we do not want. Him we can do without. We can make it our own way. The adverb is different, but the end is the same — restless withering, drunken withering, religious, secular, or thoughtless withering . Some overdose on pleasure. Others get high on their own morality. Still others distract themselves from death’s shadow creeping over them with fantasy football and rounds of golf. But for all that, withering. But Jesus himself asserts that he is the Tree. He is the one we were made for; in him alone can we find the life that haunts us in still and sober moments. Be grafted to him through repentance and faith, be attached to him by the Spirit of the living God, have his words live in you, direct you, amaze you, and dead things will come to life. And what will it be on that day, I am compelled to continue, for those dry and fruitless branches who refused life in him? They will be gathered and thrown into the fire and burned as useless things. But Jesus came that you might have otherwise. He told us his mission was to bring life — life abundantly . Imagine the branch grafted to the tree, suddenly infused with life and purpose and the vital sap of God’s own Spirit. We are as branches; the Father, Son, and Spirit are the source of everlasting life. With him, we flourish though all may seem to go poorly. Without him, only sapped wood remains. Would you like to know more about this Jesus? Now, I tell you this to highlight one of many places where the Bible addresses the interiority of man and its solution: God. I want you to see how dangerous the alternative answers found in modern therapeutic culture are to our souls and our churches. It is a scourge, especially to this inward age, not because a therapeutic culture takes distresses of the heart seriously, but because it too often sends branches reaching out for anything but the Tree. Ingrown Toenails The problem comes not from a focus on the inner man. Anyone who says the Bible has little to say about internal battles, demons, depressions, anxieties, doubts, and the despairs of human life should not air his ignorance. The Scriptures abound with stories of the faithful brought into all the perplexities and pains of life in a fallen world. The Psalms, as one profound example, give u

title: Scrolling the Soul Shallow
summary: Entertainment swamps nearly all of life in triviality. So, how can we resist the tide and embrace a wholehearted, soul-satisfying pursuit of God? Listen Now
summary_zh: 娱乐将生活的几乎所有方面都淹没在琐碎之中。那么，我们该如何抵挡这股潮流，全心全意地追求神，让灵魂得到满足呢？马上收听
title_zh: 滚动灵魂浅滩
content: Audio Transcript We lived through a decade of smartphone abuse and overuse (roughly 2015 to 2024). We talked at length about it on this podcast. I wrote books about it. Most of us have come to terms with when and where we’ve been online too much. We lament the wasted time, knowing we should have been doing more important things. The clock sped up as we lost ourselves in the everlasting scroll of eye-grabbing images and video. But what if time was not the greatest cost? What if something more serious happened to us, a lingering damage still present inside of us now? Today on Ask Pastor John: scrolling the soul shallow. It’s a question from Noah, a young man in Akron, Ohio. “Pastor John, I have made Titus 2:6–8 my aim as a young man. I know Paul is speaking to a young pastor. I am not a pastor, but I want to be self-controlled. I want to show myself ‘to be a model of good works,’ and I want to display ‘integrity, dignity, and sound speech.’ The main struggle I face is the shallowness of the culture in which we live. On my phone, computer, and TV, I see endless examples of flippancy. That’s really all I see some days. The whole world seems bent on numbing our souls to eternal realities. How can a young man resist all this and stay spiritually alert and cultivate these virtues?” One of the reasons I love this question is because I have said many times that the worst problem with television (or now let’s just say Instagram or any online media in general) is probably not the pervasive sexualization of all of life — that’s big enough — but rather the pervasive trivialization of all of life. You can scarcely watch TV ads or be online for more than ten seconds without being dump-trucked with banality and silliness. Grown men and women, even famous grown men and women, act like eleven-year-olds whose high point at summer camp was to bob for apples in a toilet filled with Mello Yello — the apex of satisfaction. That’s the quality that we’re being dumped on every day. This is the world we live in: silliness, humor, fun, joking, casual, flippant, cleverness, whimsical. And all that has made its way tragically into parenting, worship services, preaching, and hosting an event, even a serious one. Many modern people have never tasted serious joy, glad gravity, happy earnestness, or joyful weightiness. They have no category for such a thing. There’s fun and there’s boredom. That’s it. Life is that shallow, that insignificant. So, Noah asks, “How can I resist all this? How can I march to the beat of a different drummer?” 1. Distinguish between joy and fun. First, make sure that you are clear that joy and fun are not identical. Today, the word fun has virtually taken over the experience of serious joy. “Think about the shortness of life and the inevitability of death and the great realities of God.” Fun is what you have when playing with your kids on the living-room floor, flag football with the guys on Saturday, or a day at Disney World. That’s fun — nothing wrong with it. But now, church planting is fun, worship services are fun, Bible studies are fun. It’s as if you learn the language of trees while walking among twenty-foot Georgia pines, and then you visit three-hundred-foot, two-thousand-year-old redwoods in California and you have no language. They’re just fun trees. They’re not magnificent. They’re not breathtaking. They’re not humbling. They’re just fun trees. So, Noah, grow your vocabulary of joy and significance and wonder, because more often than we would like to admit, the heart shrinks to the language we have to express it rather than the other way around. If you call enough magnificent things “fun,” before long, that’s all they’ll be. Your heart will have shrunk to your vocabulary. 2. Know you’re not crazy. Second, listen to the warnings of Scripture to know you’re not crazy. The Bible is very aware of people who are incapable of being happily serious, and all their language is just clever or joking or trifling. - “Like a madman w

音频记录 我们经历了十年的智能手机虐待和过度使用(大约2015年到2024年). 我们在播客上详细谈论了这个问题。 我写过书 我们大部分人都同意我们上网的时间和地点。 我们对浪费时间感到遗憾,因为我们知道我们应该做更重要的事。

时钟加速了,因为我们迷失了自己 在永恒的卷轴 挖眼影像和视频。 但如果时间不是最大的代价呢? 如果更严重的事情发生在我们身上, 那现在我们体内仍然存在的伤害呢? 今天在"问约翰牧师"上:滚动灵魂浅浅. 俄亥俄州Akron的年轻人Noah问:

“约翰神父,我把提图斯2:6-8作为我作为年轻人的目标。 我知道保罗在和一个年轻的牧师说话 我不是牧师,但我想自我控制。 我想展示自己“成为优秀作品的典范”, 我面临的主要斗争是我们所生活的文化的浅浅.

在我的手机、电脑和电视上, 我看到无尽的翻转例子。 这些日子我只看到这些。 整个世界似乎都想把我们的灵魂麻木于永恒的现实。

一个年轻人怎么能抗拒这一切,保持精神警惕,培养这些美德呢?” 我喜欢这个问题的原因之一 是因为我已经说过很多次了 电视最糟糕的问题(或者现在我们只说Instagram或任何一般的网络媒体) 可能不是 普遍的性化 生活的所有 - 这已经够大了 - 而是 普遍的轻视所有o

f 寿. 你几乎不能看电视广告 或在线超过十秒 而不被垃圾车 与平庸和愚蠢。 长大的男女,甚至著名的成年男女,都表现得像11岁的孩子,他们在夏令营的高潮是在充满了梅洛·耶洛的厕所里为苹果吹嘘——满足的顶峰. 这就是我们每天被抛弃的质量。

这就是我们生活的世界: 愚蠢、幽默、有趣、开玩笑、随意、放荡、聪明、狂喜。 在养育子女、礼拜、传教和主持活动,甚至是严肃的活动方面,所有这一切都是可悲的。 许多现代人从未品尝过严肃的喜悦,快乐的引力,快乐的真诚,或者欢乐的重量. 他们没有这样的分类。

有乐趣和无聊。 就这样。 生命是那么浅,那么微不足道。 诺亚问道:我怎能抗拒这一切呢? 我怎能走向一个不同的鼓手呢?” 1.区分欢喜乐. 第一,确保你明白快乐和乐趣并不相同。 今天,乐趣一词几乎取代了严肃的欢乐经历.

“考虑到生命的短暂性、死亡的必然性和上帝的伟大现实。” 有趣的是,当你在客厅地板上和孩子们玩时, 星期六和男生一起打橄榄球, 或者一天在迪士尼世界。 这很有趣, 但现在,教堂的栽培是乐趣,礼拜服务是乐趣,圣经研究是乐趣.

就像在二十英尺高的乔治亚松林中学习树木语言, 他们只是有趣的树。 他们并不伟大。 他们并不令人惊叹。 他们不会发抖。 他们只是有趣的树。

所以,诺亚, 增加你的喜悦和意义 和奇异的词汇, 因为比我们想承认的更多时候, 心脏收缩到 语言 我们必须表达它而不是相反。 如果你在不久之前就称它为“有趣”的话, 你的心会缩到词汇里 2. 知道你没有疯。

第二,听从圣经的警告, 圣经中非常了解那些不能快乐严肃的人,他们所有的语言都只是聪明或开玩笑,或三思而行. - 像个疯子

content: The following is the substance of a pamphlet published by Archibald G. Brown, a student and then great ally of C. H. Spurgeon in the cause of the gospel in London. Brown here draws attention to a practice that was gaining ground in the churches of his day: that of holding ‘amusements’ of various kinds, which obscured, diverted from, and in some cases replaced the proper ministry of local churches. Brown was savagely attacked in the wake of the publication of the pamphlet, derided as ‘a kill-joy,’ ‘a morbid pietist,’ and ‘a sour bigot.’ His meaning, however, had been deliberately misrepresented. 1 Brown nowhere objects to all amusement per se , but amusement which masquerades as ministry, distracting the church and deceiving needy sinners. While the context in which Brown wrote may be different from ours, we need to hear his burden for a Church—and for Christians—to make a decisive break with the world and its practices. An Evil in the Camp of the Lord DIFFERENT days demand their own special testimony. The watchman who would be faithful to his Lord and the City of his God has need to carefully note the signs of the times and emphasize his witness accordingly. Con­cerning the testimony needed now, there can the little, if any, doubt. An evil is in the professed camp of the Lord—so gross, so brazen in its impudence—that the most short-sighted of spiritual men can hardly fail to notice it. During the past few years it has developed at an ab­normal rate, ever for evil. It has worked like leaven until now the whole lump ferments. Look which way you may, its presence makes itself manifest. There is little if any­thing, to choose between Church, Chapel, or Mission Hall. However they may differ in some respects, they bear a striking likeness in the posters that figure upon and dis­figure their notice boards. Amusement for the people i s the leading article advertised by each. If any of my readers doubt my statement, or think my utterance too sweeping, let them take a tour of inspection and study “the announce­ments for the week” at the doors of the sanctuaries of the neighbourhood; or let them read the religious advertise­ments in their local papers. I have done this again and again, until the hideous fact has been proved up to the hilt, that “amusement” is ousting the preaching of the gospel as the great attraction: “Concerts,” “Entertain­ments,” “Fancy Fairs,” “Smoking Conferences,” “Dramatic Performances,” are the words honoured with biggest type and most startling colours. The burden of the Lord is upon me in this matter The Concert is fast becoming as much a recognised part of church life as the Prayer Meeting, and is already, in most places, far better attended. “Providing recreation for the people” will soon be looked upon as a necessary part of Christian work and as binding upon the Church of God, as though it were a Divine command, unless some strong voices be raised which will make themselves heard. I do not presume to possess such a voice, but I do entertain the hope that I may awaken some louder echoes. Anyway, the burden of the Lord is upon me in this matter, and I leave it with Him to give my testimony ringing tone, or to let it die away in silence. I shall have delivered my soul in either case. Yet the conviction fills my mind that in all parts of the country there are faithful men and women who see the danger and deplore it and will endorse my witness and my warning. Gratifying the Flesh and Retaining a Comfortable Conscience It is only during the past few years that “amusement” has become a recognized weapon of our warfare and de­veloped into a mission. There has been a steady “down grade” in this respect. From “speaking out,” as the Puri­tans did, the Church has gradually toned down her testi­mony; then winked at and excused the frivolities of the day. 以下是阿奇博尔德·G·布朗(Archibald G. Brown)出版的一本小册子的实质内容,他是一个学生,后来成为了C·H·斯普亨在伦敦福音书事业中的重要盟友. Brown提醒大家注意他当时的教会日益盛行的一种做法:举行各种 " 纪念会 " 的做法,这种做法模糊不清,转移了注意力,有时还取代了当地教会的适当部会。

Brown在小册子发表后遭到野蛮攻击, 然而,他的意思被蓄意歪曲。 1 布朗无处反对所有娱乐本身, 但娱乐伪装成牧师, 分散教会的注意力 欺骗需要的罪人。

虽然布朗写作的背景可能与我们不同,但我们需要听取他对于一个教会——以及基督徒——的责任,以便同世界及其做法决裂。 魔王营里的恶魔 要求他们自己作证

忠于他的主和他所崇拜的城市的守望者,必须仔细记取时代的迹象,并相应地强调他的见证. 在现在所需要的证词中,可以有一点怀疑。 主所宣示的营中,有恶行;主的营中,有恶行;主的营中,有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行;有恶行。

在过去几年里,它以异常的速度发展,永远是邪恶的。 直到现在,它一直工作着,就像离开一样。 看看你们可以走哪条路,它的存在就变得明显了。 教会、礼拜堂或传教堂之间几乎没有任何选择。

然而,它们在某些方面可能有所不同,它们在海报上带有惊人的相似性,这些海报上显示它们的通知板并毁容。 为人民提供娱乐 我是每篇广告的主要文章

如果我的读者怀疑我的发言,或者认为我的言论过于笼统,让他们巡视视察,在附近圣所门口研究“一周的公告”;或者让他们在当地报纸上阅读宗教广告。

在令人发指的事实被证实之前,我一再这样做,即“辱骂”正在驱使福音的传道成为伟大的取景:“关注”、“参与”、“盛会”、“吸烟会”、“戏剧表演”是用最出名和最令人惊叹的颜色表达的言论。

主的重担在我这里 音乐会正迅速成为教会生活中 公认的部分 与祈祷会一样 并且已经,在大多数地方,

“为人民提供娱乐”将很快被视为基督教工作的必要部分,对上帝的教会具有约束力,似乎这是神的命令,除非有人发出强烈的声音,让自己听到。 我并不认为拥有这种声音,但我确实希望能够唤起一些更响亮的回声。

无论如何,上帝的重任 由我负责这件事, 我留给他 让我的证词响亮的语气, 或者让它静静地死去。 无论哪种情况,我都会送出我的灵魂 然而,这一信念使我满怀信心,即全国各地都有忠实的男女看到这种危险并对此感到痛惜,并将赞同我的证人和我的警告。

修行并保持舒适的良知 直到过去几年,“暴行”才成为我们战争的公认武器并发展成一个特派团。 这方面的“级别”稳步下降。 正如普里坦人所做的那样,教会从“大声疾呼”开始,逐渐淡出她的遗言;然后轻视并原谅了今天的纷争。

然后,她在边境上容忍他们,现在她收养了他们,在“影响群众,让人民听到他们的声音”的恳求下,为他们提供了家园。

title: Pitfalls in Preaching: A Letter on Application
source: Banner of Truth · 教会历史
summary: The following letter was published in the December 2025 issue of the Banner Magazine. It is published here at the request of a reader who found it helpful, in the hope that its counsel might be blessed to others also. You can also listen to a reading of this letter on the Banner Podcast. Dear […]   The post  Pitfalls in Preaching: A Letter on Application  appeared first on  Banner of Truth USA .
summary_zh: 以下信件发表在2025年12月的《旗帜》杂志上。这本书是应一位读者的要求出版的，他认为这本书很有帮助，希望它的忠告也能祝福他人。您也可以在Banner播客上收听这封信的阅读。尊敬的[…]《讲道中的陷阱：一封关于申请的信》（ Pitfalls in Preaching: A Letter on Application ）一文首次出现在美国真理旗帜
title_zh: 讲道中的陷阱：一封关于申请的信
content: The following letter was published in the December 2025 issue of the Banner Magazine. It is published here at the request of a reader who found it helpful, in the hope that its counsel might be blessed to others also. You can also listen to a reading of this letter on the Banner Podcast. Dear J______, Following our conversation about application in preaching, I thought I would send along some thoughts I have had over the years on the subject. I want to point out some pitfalls you may want to keep in mind as you train R______. The only reason I know about them is from spending too much time in them myself! There has been a lot of self–examination and repenting over the years for me in this matter. The first thought is that too often (even in some of the best books on preaching) we hear that the text drives the sermon. This is a half-truth. A potentially dangerous half-truth. I have seen a man so intent on expositing his text well (and he did it very well) that he did not seem to notice or care that a third of the people in the room walked out before he finished preaching because he went on so long and the last meal of the conference was being served to meet the constraint of local train times. A wrong type of focus on the text and its explanation can make us oblivious to the very people the text is for. A preacher who stands up to preach having spent ninety per cent of his sermon preparation time in the week concentrating on the biblical text has not sufficiently realized what preaching actually is. In their book Letters Along the Way D. A. Carson and John Woodbridge put it this way: A chief reason why so much of what passes for evangelical expository preaching is so boring and irrelevant is that the preacher has spent a vastly disproportionate amount of preparation time in exegesis and outlines, and so little in thinking through how the Word of God is to wound and heal (to use the language of Hosea). 1 So preaching is about people. Preaching is about what God has to say to people about their lives . The text for a sermon is what God has to say to people . So the text of a sermon is like the recipe for a dish. A good cook would never be so focused on a recipe that she did not stop to realize that this was not at all the type of food her guests would need or appreciate. She would have her guests in mind from the start. After all, the goal of a good cook is not simply a matter of a recipe or a certain dish. It is feeding and feasting people . People drive the sermon. People are the reason God has given us the message in the biblical text. The biblical text leads the preacher to what the people need to hear from God. But the biblical text is only a means . The goal is people—to bring them somewhere that God wants them to go. To enlighten them, change them, help them, console them, correct them, train them to worship and serve God. People-oriented preaching comes from a God-centred, loving interest in them . Text-oriented preaching may simply come from the preacher’s love for preaching, for exegesis or for theology. A physician may be fascinated by medical treatments. But the good physician’s real interest is not treatments but people whose suffering has called for those treatments. Just so, true preaching is about people. That brings me to a second, related thought. We are often told that in preparing a sermon the key is finding the main idea of the text. To consider this as the key is not a people-oriented point of view and does not produce good preaching. It produces preaching with lots of emphasis on ideas and little emphasis on application. The key to preparing a sermon is not to find the main idea of the text. It is to find the main goal of the text. Not ‘What does the biblical text mainly say?’ But rather ‘What does this text intend to mainly do for people?’ What does the text intend mainly to effect in the lives of people? What does this text aim to move the people to believe, to do, to become? Application! A. T. Pierson, i
content_zh: 以下信件发表于"班纳杂志"2025年12月号. 它应一位读者的要求在这里出版,他觉得它很有帮助,希望它的律师也能得到他人的祝福。 也可以在"班纳·波德克特"上收听对这封信的读取. 亲爱的J-,在我们讨论申请布道后,我想,我将提出一些多年来我对这一问题的看法。 我想指出一些陷阱 你可能想记住 当你训练R. 我了解他们的唯一原因 就是自己花太多时间在他们身上 多年来,我一直以来都在自责自悔。 第一种想法是,太多时候(即使在一些关于布道的好书中),我们听到文字驱动布道. 这是半个事实。 一个潜在的危险 半真相。 我见过一个男人如此有意地公开他的文字(他做得非常好),他似乎没有注意到或关心房间里有三分之一的人在他完成布道之前就离开,因为他走了这么长一段时间,会议的最后一餐是用来应付当地火车时间的限制。 错误地注重案文及其解释会使我们忘记案文所要为的人。 一位挺身而出进行传道的传道者,在一周里,他90%的布道准备时间都集中在圣经文本上,但是他没有充分意识到实际的传道内容。 在他们所著的"沿着路"(Letrys A. A. Carson)和"约翰·伍德布里奇"(John Woodbridge)一书中这样写道: 传福音的宣讲之所以如此之多,实在是无趣而无关紧要的一个主要原因是,传道人花费了大量的不相称的准备时间来解剖和提纲,在思考"上帝之道"是怎样去伤口和愈合(使用"霍西"的语言)时却很少考虑. 1个 故传道以人为事. 意义在于上帝要对人们说 他们的生活 讲道的文字是上帝要对人们说的话。 所以布道的文字就像菜谱。 一个好厨师永远也不会把注意力集中在一个配方上,以至于她不禁意识到这根本不是客人需要或欣赏的食物类型. 她一开始就想着她的客人 毕竟,一个好厨师的目标不仅仅是一个菜谱或某种菜肴的问题. 它在给人们提供食物和盛宴。 人们驱使布道。 人们是上帝给我们圣经文本中的信息的原因。 圣经文本将传道人引向人们需要从上帝那里听到的. 但圣经文本只是一个手段。 目标是人们,把他们带到上帝要他们去的地方去。 为了启蒙他们,改变他们,帮助他们,安慰他们,矫正他们,训练他们去崇拜并服务于上帝. 以人为中心的布道来自以上帝为中心, 以文字为取向的传道可能只是来自传道者对传道、开教或神学的热爱。 医生可能因治疗而着迷。 但好医生的真正兴趣不是治疗,而是那些遭受痛苦需要治疗的人。 所以,真正的传道是关于人的。 这让我想到另一个相关的想法。 我们经常被告知,在准备布道时,关键在于找到案文的主要想法。 将此视为关键不是以人民为导向的观点,也不产生好传道. 它产生许多强调思想的布道,很少强调应用。 准备布道的关键不是找到文本的主要想法. 它是为了找到案文的主要目标。 而非"圣经主要说些什么?" 但更确切地说,“这个文本主要是为了什么?” 案文主要打算如何影响人们的生活? 这个文字的目的是要促使人们相信,去做,变成什么? 申请! A. T. 皮尔逊,i
