title_zh: Patrick Nagatani：通过色彩、摄影和艺术进行的精神探索
content: Arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 2009, I was fortunate to catch the final chapter of artist and photographer Patrick Nagatani’ s remarkable career before his death from cancer in 2017. As one of my favorite modern photographers, Nagatani fascinated me with his unique artistic vision, his imaginative compositions, and his ability to transform his photography into extraordinary works of art. Watching him at gallery openings was a pleasure. He was cordial, kind, and genuinely responsive to those who engaged him. There was something refreshing about an artist of his stature who remained approachable, thoughtful, and seemingly delighted to discuss his work. An Artist Shaped by History Photo credit: Grahm Howe, 1979. Patrick Ryoichi Nagatani was born on August 19, 1945, in Chicago, Illinois, only days after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. His Japanese American parents had experienced incarceration during World War II, and the legacy of displacement, cultural identity, and nuclear destruction would profoundly influence his artistic imagination. Raised Catholic, Nagatani eventually moved with his family to Los Angeles. He studied at UCLA, earning his Master of Fine Arts in 1980. His early professional experience included model-making for Hollywood productions, helping establish the theatrical techniques that later distinguished his photography. In 1987, he moved to Albuquerque to teach at the University of New Mexico , where he became an influential professor and internationally recognized artist. His celebrated Nuclear Enchantment series examined the disturbing relationship between New Mexico’s landscapes and the nuclear industry. Other projects investigated Japanese American incarceration, archaeology, cultural memory, and the uncertainty of photographic truth. ‘Generation to Generation’, Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) Nuclear Powered Vehicles, West Mesa, Albuquerque, New Mexico, 1991 & 1993, Chromogenic print (Ilfocolor Deluxe), 17 X 22 and 27 3/4 X 34 1/4 My interest in Nagatani extends beyond the artistry of his photographs—the theatrical tableaux, vibrant colors, and beautifully constructed compositions—to what I perceive as an underlying spiritual search. Throughout his career, questions of identity, mortality, healing, and transcendence surfaced repeatedly. Though not every work was explicitly religious, I suggest that there’s a longing to discover meaning beyond the material world. One early example is his series Colorful Cathedrals (1980–1983), which invites consideration of the relationship between artistic creation and spiritual imagination. Colorful Cathedrals: Light and the Sacred Nagatani’s Colorful Cathedrals emerged during his early experimentation with color photography and constructed imagery. The series was exhibited in Los Angeles and elsewhere, including a 1983 exhibition at the Arco Center for Visual Arts. His artistic practice during this period involved manipulating photographic environments rather than merely documenting existing scenes. Using constructed arrangements, controlled lighting, and photographic experimentation, he explored how color could transform visual experience. Canterbury #1, Kent, England, 1981, 36 X 33 X 2 1/2, nine P-12 Cibachrome prints from original SX-70’s with mixed media (oils, enamels, watercolors, sprayed and selectively hand colored) For me, the title of the series suggests something spiritually evocative. Cathedrals have historically served as architectural expressions of Christian theology, with light and color—particularly through stained glass—symbolizing divine illumination. Having graduated at Canterbury Christchurch University, with an Evensong service at Canterbury Cathedral, I’m drawn to his “Canterbury #1” work. Patrick Nagatani juxtaposes the grandeur of a Gothic cathedral with human hands holding yellow cards, suggesting a tension between sacred architecture and humanity’s search for spiritual meaning. 2009年抵达新墨西哥州阿尔布开克, 我有幸在2017年因癌症去世前, 作为我最喜欢的现代摄影师之一,那加塔尼用他独特的艺术眼光,想象力的构思,以及把他的摄影改造为非凡的艺术作品的能力,让我着迷.

在画廊的开幕式上看着他真是荣幸 他对雇用他的人是真诚、善良和真诚的。 有一些令人振奋的东西 关于他的地位 艺术家保持接触, 深思熟虑, 似乎很高兴讨论他的作品。 An Artist shaped by History Photo credit: Grahm Howe, 1979 (英语).

帕特里克·里约伊奇·纳加塔尼于1945年8月19日出生于伊利诺伊州芝加哥,距广岛和长崎原子弹爆炸仅几天后. 他的日本裔美国父母在二战期间曾遭受过监禁,流离失所,文化认同和核毁灭的遗留影响将深刻影响他的艺术想象.

养成天主教徒,那加塔尼最终随家人移居洛杉矶. 他在加州大学洛杉矶分校学习,1980年挣得他的美术硕士. 他早期的专业经验包括为好莱坞的制作制作模特,帮助建立后来将他的摄影区分开的戏剧技术.

1987年,他搬到阿尔伯克基,在新墨西哥大学任教,在那里他成为了一位有影响力的教授和国际知名的艺术家. 他的著名的"核魅力"系列研究了新墨西哥州地貌与核工业之间的令人不安的关系.

其他项目调查了日本裔美国人的监禁,考古,文化记忆,以及照片真相的不确定性.

一个早期的例子就是他的系列"彩色大教堂"(1980年-1983年),这请人们考虑艺术创作与精神想象之间的关系. 彩色大教堂:光明与圣洁的那加塔尼的彩色大教堂在他早期的彩色摄影和构筑图像实验中出现.

该系列在洛杉矶和其他地方展出,包括1983年在Arco视觉艺术中心展出. 他在此期间的艺术实践涉及操纵摄影环境,而不仅仅是记录现有的场景. 他利用构建的安排,受控的照明,以及摄影实验,探索了色彩如何转化视觉体验.
